Learning objectives

Nervous-system overview: distinguish CNS and PNS. Spinal cord: (1) longitudinal and internal organization, (2) spinal nerve formation and branches, (3) cord/vertebral alignment and herniated discs, (4) meninges/spaces, (5) afferents and dermatomes/shingles, (6) efferents and myotomes/reflexes, (7) LP and epidural anatomy, (8) vascular supply and drainage, (9) imaging anatomy.

BIG PICTUREThink in three linked maps: where is it? (vertebral level, root, nerve, space, vascular territory) → what does it carry? (sensory, motor, CSF, blood) → what goes wrong? (radicular deficit, reflex change, dermatomal rash, cauda equina syndrome, vascular injury).
Learning objective 0

Nervous-system organization and terminology

Central nervous system (CNS) = brain and spinal cord, which integrate information. Peripheral nervous system (PNS) = cranial nerves, spinal nerves, and ganglia, which link the CNS to receptors and effectors. Afferent travels toward the CNS; efferent travels away. Somatic refers primarily to body wall/limbs; visceral to organs.

ConceptCNS termPNS term
Cluster of neuronal cell bodiesNucleus; spinal cord longitudinal collection = columnGanglion (e.g., dorsal root ganglion)
Bundle of axonsTract / fasciculus / lemniscus; grouped tracts = funiculusNerve / root / ramus
Support cellsAstrocytes, microglia, ependymal cells, oligodendrocytesSchwann and satellite cells
FOUNDATIONS LINKA neuronal soma maintains the cell, dendrites receive input, and axons conduct signals to terminals. Myelin increases conduction velocity. This cellular pattern helps explain why motor cell bodies reside in the spinal cord while sensory cell bodies sit in dorsal root ganglia.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What is the difference between a nucleus and a ganglion?
Both are collections of neuronal cell bodies; a nucleus is in the CNS and a ganglion is in the PNS.
Learning objective 1

Longitudinal and internal anatomy of the spinal cord

The spinal cord continues from the medulla at the foramen magnum, travels inside the vertebral canal, and ends near the L1–L2 vertebral level in adults. It is a conduction pathway for ascending sensory and descending motor information and a center for spinal reflexes.

Cross-sectional orientation: the posterior median sulcus is shallow; the anterior median fissure is deeper. Sensory input enters posteriorly; motor output leaves anteriorly. Gray matter forms a central butterfly/H shape, and white matter occupies the periphery.

RegionStructureCore role
Gray matterPosterior/dorsal hornReceives/processes somatic and visceral afferent signals
Gray matterAnterior/ventral hornLower motor neuron cell bodies → skeletal muscle
Gray matterLateral autonomic cell columnPreganglionic visceral motor neurons
White matterPosterior funiculusAscending sensory tracts
White matterAnterior & lateral funiculiAscending sensory + descending motor tracts
White matterAnterior white commissureCrossing fibers
MUST KNOWAscending = sensory → brain (lecture uses first-, second-, and third-order neurons). Descending = motor command → spinal cord → peripheral motor output (upper and lower motor neurons).
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · You see large ventral horns and relatively less surrounding white matter. Which level is likely compared with a high cervical section?
A lumbar or sacral enlargement level, because motor pools for limbs enlarge the gray matter and white-matter proportion generally falls caudally.
Learning objective 2

Spinal nerves: roots, mixed nerves and rami

Rootlets merge into roots: dorsal rootlets → dorsal root (sensory), and ventral rootlets → ventral root (motor). The dorsal root ganglion contains the sensory neuron cell bodies. Dorsal and ventral roots join into a short mixed spinal nerve, which then divides into dorsal and ventral rami—both of which remain mixed.

SegmentWhat travels in it?Where?
Dorsal rootSensory (afferent)Enters cord via posterior rootlets; DRG cell bodies
Ventral rootMotor (efferent), including applicable autonomic efferentsLeaves anterior spinal cord
Short spinal nerveBothRoots unite near intervertebral foramen
Dorsal ramusBothDeep intrinsic back muscles and skin of back
Ventral ramusBothMost anterolateral trunk and limbs; forms major nerve plexuses at many levels
EXAM TRAPVentral root ≠ ventral ramus. A ventral root is motor-only; a ventral ramus contains BOTH sensory and motor fibers. A dorsal root is sensory-only; a dorsal ramus is mixed.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A lesion of the dorsal ramus versus the dorsal root: which one can damage motor supply to deep back muscles?
The dorsal ramus, because it is a mixed branch; the dorsal root is a sensory root.
Learning objective 3

Spinal cord segments, vertebrae and disc herniation

There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal. A spinal cord segment is not the same as a vertebral level. During development, the vertebral column outgrows the cord; lower nerve roots descend through the canal to reach their exit foramina, forming the cauda equina below the conus.

Common posterolateral disc herniation compresses the traversing nerve root in the lumbar spine: L4–L5 disc → L5 root; L5–S1 disc → S1 root. The handout also explicitly notes common cervical patterns: C5–C6 disc → C6 root, C6–C7 disc → C7 root. The direction and position of the herniation matter; these are the course's typical examples, not every possible disc lesion.

CLINICAL CONNECTIONRadiculopathy = compression/inflammation of a nerve root producing segmental pain, paresthesias, weakness and/or altered reflexes. Cauda equina syndrome is an emergency: urinary retention or incontinence, saddle anesthesia, bilateral/multiroot weakness and bowel dysfunction are red flags.
COMMON CONFUSIONThe spinal cord terminates near vertebral L1–L2, but lumbar and sacral nerve roots extend below that level in the cauda equina. A lumbar puncture at L3–L4 or L4–L5 enters a cistern with roots, not the cord itself.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A patient has typical posterolateral L5–S1 disc herniation. Which nerve root is most likely affected?
S1 (the traversing root at this disc level).
Learning objective 4

Spinal meninges and clinically important spaces

From outside to inside: epidural space → dura mater → potential subdural space → arachnoid mater → CSF-containing subarachnoid space → pia mater → spinal cord. The outer tough dura forms the thecal sac; the pia adheres directly to neural tissue, extends as the filum terminale internum, and makes denticulate ligaments that stabilize the cord.

Space/layerEssential contentClinical meaning
Epidural spaceFat; internal vertebral venous plexusSite of epidural anesthesia
Dura materOuter strong sheathMust be passed to reach CSF
Subdural spacePotential spaceNot the intended CSF sampling compartment
Arachnoid materDelicate middle meninxCrossed during lumbar puncture
Subarachnoid spaceCSF, vessels; lumbar cistern caudallySite of lumbar puncture sample
Pia materAdherent innermost meninxDenticulate ligaments, filum terminale
MUST KNOWAdult conus medullaris ≈ L1–L2; the dural sac and lumbar cistern extend to about S2 per the handout. This creates a lumbar CSF access compartment below the cord.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which space contains cerebrospinal fluid, and which space contains epidural fat and internal vertebral veins?
CSF is in subarachnoid space; fat and internal vertebral veins are in epidural space.
Learning objective 5

Afferent sensory fibers, dermatomes and shingles

General somatic sensation (touch, pain, temperature, vibration, proprioception) flows peripheral receptor → pseudounipolar sensory neuron → dorsal root ganglion → dorsal root → dorsal horn/CNS. A dermatome is a segmental unilateral skin territory associated with a particular spinal nerve/root. Adjacent dermatomes overlap.

The peripheral cutaneous nerves shown in the slides are multisegmental: for example, lateral antebrachial cutaneous (C5–C7) and lateral femoral cutaneous (L2–L3). A named peripheral nerve often contains fibers that were reshuffled by a plexus rather than representing one root.

FIRST AID CONNECTIONThe high-yield reasoning link is latent VZV in a dorsal root or cranial sensory ganglion → reactivation along sensory fibers → unilateral dermatomal vesicular eruption. The sensory geography identifies the affected ganglion/root rather than a named peripheral nerve.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Sensory loss follows the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve territory rather than one segmental stripe. Is a single spinal root or named peripheral nerve a better first localization?
A named peripheral nerve; root distributions are dermatomal, whereas cutaneous nerves commonly mix root contributions.
Learning objective 6

Efferent motor fibers, myotomes and reflex arcs

Somatic motor output follows a lower motor neuron whose cell body lies in the ventral horn; its axon exits by the ventral root to reach skeletal muscle through the mixed spinal nerve and peripheral branches. A myotome groups muscle actions by their spinal root contribution. An action can receive fibers from more than one root and travel through a named peripheral nerve.

Reflex = rapid involuntary response to a stimulus. The lecture's five-part reflex arc: 1 receptor/stimulus → 2 sensory neuron → 3 spinal cord integration → 4 motor neuron → 5 effector. The stretch (deep tendon/myotatic) reflex uses a stretched muscle to elicit contraction.

FIRST AID CONNECTIONLocalize before naming a reflex: root/afferent failure, spinal integration failure or efferent lower-motor failure can all reduce a deep tendon reflex. An upper motor neuron lesion can produce hyperreflexia after the acute phase, because descending regulation is impaired.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A stretch reflex begins at a muscle spindle. List the next four main elements in the reflex arc.
Sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → skeletal muscle effector.
Learning objective 7

Lumbar puncture versus epidural anesthesia

Lumbar puncture obtains CSF from the lumbar cistern, typically at L3–L4 or L4–L5; the superior iliac crests orient the examiner near L4. With a midline approach, the needle progresses toward the subarachnoid space below the adult conus. Epidural anesthesia delivers medication into the epidural space to block nearby spinal nerve roots without intentionally puncturing dura/arachnoid.

MUST KNOWLP midline sequence used in the appended handout: skin → subcutaneous tissue → supraspinous ligament → interspinous ligament → ligamentum flavum → epidural space → dura → arachnoid → subarachnoid space. The slide adds a muscle step; see the source-difference audit.
CLINICAL CONNECTIONThe lecture handout cautions against lumbar puncture when increased intracranial pressure raises risk; clinically, the contraindication depends on the cause and signs of mass effect/obstruction, so this is a safety consideration rather than a universal rule that any elevated pressure forbids LP.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What tissue separates the intended endpoint of an epidural injection from the intended endpoint of a lumbar puncture?
The dura and arachnoid: epidural injections stop superficial to dura; LP crosses them to reach subarachnoid CSF.
Learning objective 8

Spinal cord arteries, veins and clinical vulnerability

There are three longitudinal spinal arteries: one anterior spinal artery (unpaired; supplied by vertebral branches) serving the anterior two-thirds of the cord, and two posterior spinal arteries serving the posterior one-third. Segmental medullary and radicular arteries reinforce this blood supply.

The great anterior segmental medullary artery (Adamkiewicz) is an especially important contribution to lower spinal cord perfusion. It frequently arises on the left (slide states roughly 65%) and is vulnerable during some aortic procedures. Loss of supply can produce major lower-extremity neurologic deficits and sphincter dysfunction.

FIRST AID CONNECTIONVascular neuroanatomy helps predict deficit patterns: an anterior spinal artery territory injury often affects motor pathways and pain/temperature pathways while posterior-column functions can be relatively spared. This is an additional board localization connection, not a claim that the professor explicitly taught the full syndrome.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which artery supplies most of the anterior cord, and what feature makes Batson plexus clinically important?
Anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds; valveless Batson plexus permits communication with pelvic/other veins and can facilitate spread of metastases or infection.
Learning objective 9

Imaging and practical identification

The learning objective explicitly asks for identification on x-ray, MRI and CT. The slide deck illustrates several anatomical cuts and a sagittal T2-weighted lumbar MRI (slide 28), but does not provide a comprehensive labeled CT or x-ray image atlas. Identify what the supplied figures actually show rather than assuming additional imaging conventions were covered.

PRACTICAL IMAGEWithout labels, be able to identify: anterior vs posterior side; H-shaped central gray matter; dorsal and ventral horns; conus vs cauda equina; dorsal root ganglion; exiting spinal nerve; epidural fat vs CSF-containing subarachnoid space; and the three spinal artery territories.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · On a sagittal lumbar MRI at the L4–L5 disc, what three things must you orient before attributing nerve compression to the image?
Vertebral/disc level, relation of protrusion to the canal/foramen, and the expected traversing or exiting nerve root.

Course first: the present companion captures the main slide material, incorporates directly relevant spinal-cord notes from the handout, and identifies the disagreements for checking with the professor.

Master these before moving on

1 · Dorsal root vs dorsal ramus: roots are functionally separated before they unite; both rami are mixed after the nerve forms. Essential for injury localization.
2 · Cord segments ≠ vertebral levels: adult cord ends near L1/L2 but roots continue below. Explains cauda equina and safe lumbar CSF sampling.
3 · Gray horn vs white funiculus: ventral horn houses lower motor neurons; dorsal horn receives sensory signals; funiculi carry longitudinal axons. Foundation for lesion syndromes.
4 · Dermatome vs named peripheral nerve: segmental root sensory territory versus mixed-root terminal nerve territory. Basis for differentiating radiculopathy and mononeuropathy.
5 · Epidural vs subarachnoid: anesthetic stops outside dura; LP goes through dura and arachnoid into CSF. Critical clinical anatomy.

The most useful First Aid connections

  1. VZV latency in sensory ganglia → dermatomal herpes zoster eruption.
  2. Nerve-root compression → radicular sensory, motor and reflex deficits.
  3. Cauda equina compression → saddle sensory loss and bladder/bowel dysfunction (emergency).
  4. Anterior spinal artery territory → motor and pain/temperature deficits with relative posterior-column sparing.
  5. Spinal reflex localization → compare afferent, lower motor and upper motor involvement.

These are selectively included because they extend concepts present in the lecture; they are not an additional neuroanatomy chapter.
